question: How does fire spread on fabric in microgravity?
answer:
At low airflow velocities in microgravity, flame ignited at the middle of a thin fuel spreads upstream into the oncoming airflow [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. This contrasts with normal gravity, where flames spread downstream [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Materials can also burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

In microgravity tests using fabrics such as Nomex and a 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass blend, airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s were directed along the fuel surface in opposed or concurrent directions [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. Tested fabric sample sizes included 1 to 2 cm [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. Measuring flame spread rates over thin fuels in quiescent microgravity is planned for future research [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

Our sources do not cover specific numerical flame spread rates for different fabric materials.

question: Which experiments tested oxygen levels above 30%?
answer:
Based on NASA PSI experimental data, four investigations tested oxygen concentrations above 30% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row]:

- **PSI-159 ACME CFI-G** tested oxygen levels from 12% to 85% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64].
- **PSI-10 ACME/Flame Design** tested oxygen levels from 19.8048% to 84.9978% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-10 · doi:10.60555/w4zy-bt45].
- **PSI-20 ACME BRE** tested oxygen levels from 21% to 40% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-20 · doi:10.60555/vb93-3y72].
- **PSI-69 FLEX** tested oxygen levels from 12% to 34% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

The provided sources do not report oxygen levels for several other PSI experiments (such as PSI-21, PSI-22, and PSI-26) [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

question: How was smoke detection tested on the ISS, and why does it matter?
answer:
Smoke detection was tested on the ISS using experiments such as the Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) and the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. DAFT measured background aerosol particulate levels on the station [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. SAME examined smoke particle-size distributions from solid fuels—including Teflon, Kapton, Silicone Rubber, Lampwick, and Dibutyl Phthalate—using Comparative Soot Diagnostic Hardware [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. Across 8 experimental test rows with airflows of 5–10 cm/s, SAME recorded data using smoke detectors, video cameras, thermophoretic soot samplers, and transmission electron microscopy [PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62].

This testing matters because microgravity lacks strong buoyancy-induced flows, causing smoke particles to grow larger than on Earth and altering detector responses [PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. The quantitative data provides a baseline to evaluate existing technologies and develop advanced detectors for long-duration space missions [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. Additionally, these findings help improve fire detection systems for extreme Earth environments, such as submarines [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-47 · doi:10.60555/ztgj-d202].

question: What gases were used to put out flames, and in which experiment?
answer:
Nitrogen gas was applied to extinguish flames in a drop tower test on a PMMA sphere [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

In the FLEX experiment, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, helium, and xenon were used as inert gas suppressants to study flammability limits [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. The FLEX investigation also aims to measure the effectiveness of carbon dioxide, helium, and sulfur hexafluoride gaseous suppressants [PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451]. 

The sources do not cover the exact identity of the gaseous extinguishing agent used in the BASS experiment, specifying only that an inert gaseous agent is planned to be assessed [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80].

question: What happened in the Mir fire in 1997, and what was learned?
answer:
On February 24, 1997, a fire ignited in an oxygen generating system in the Kvant-1 module aboard the Mir space station [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The searing flame lasted several minutes, filled the station's modules with toxic smoke, and blocked access to one of two Soyuz escape vehicles [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The six crew members extinguished the fire without structural damage, and Mir's life support cleared the toxic smoke over several hours with no lasting harm to the crew [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. 

Lessons learned were incorporated into the design and operations of the International Space Station (ISS) [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Russian officials updated crew emergency training, ground control response procedures, and ground preparation for solid fuel oxygen generator (SFOG) canisters [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The ISS now uses a robust oxygen generation system with dissimilar redundancies, reserving an SFOG system with added safety measures as a backup [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir].

question: Is there any fire data for Moon or Mars gravity?
answer:
The NASA PSI Data Repository contains no combustion data collected in real Moon or Mars gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. The closest PSI investigation, PSI-22, used an electric field to mimic partial gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. 

Fire data has been collected for simulated lunar gravity by burning a cotton-fiberglass blend fabric in a drop tower centrifuge [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. Additionally, the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment is planned to be performed to investigate burning materials at lunar reduced gravity [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. 

Our sources do not contain any fire data for Mars gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion].

question: What are cool flames and why are they a risk?
answer:
Cool flames are a low-temperature combustion regime that forms as an intermediate step between unreacted fuel and oxidizer, with cool diffusion flames reaching peak temperatures of 500 to 1000 K [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64]. They can form after a visible flame extinguishes and can burn for a prolonged period of time while consuming only a fraction of the vaporized fuel [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

Regarding risk, reduced-gravity environments have been shown to be particularly conducive to this low-temperature combustion regime, which impacts spacecraft fire safety concerns [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Refining the understanding of cool flame reactivity and combustion in microgravity supports the design of safer spacecraft systems [PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914]. 

Our sources do not cover the specific hazards or detailed risk mechanisms of cool flames beyond noting their association with microgravity combustion and spacecraft fire safety concerns [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914].
